Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.

# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image visibly show at least one frog placed within the toilet, rather than merely on its lid, rim, or nearby floor?
node.criteria: Pass if at least one frog is visibly situated within the toilet bowl interior, with spatial cues such as its position relative to the bowl opening and rim, contact, or occlusion supporting that it is inside rather than perched on the rim or merely overlapping the opening. Fail if the visible evidence establishes that no frog is placed within the toilet. Unknown if the relevant spatial relation cannot be resolved from the image. A frog on the lid, rim, or nearby floor alone does not establish placement within the toilet; additional frogs in those locations do not negate a genuine placement within it.
node.binding: Assess placement within the toilet shown in the edited image; do not require a particular number of frogs beyond at least one, and do not treat mere overlap with the toilet as placement within it.

node_traces.evidence: A frog is visibly situated inside the toilet bowl, below the rim and within the bowl opening. Other frogs on the lid and nearby floor do not negate this placement.

fulfillment: The node’s completion rule is too permissive for the observed edit: it treats s1 alone as sufficient, producing “complete/yes” despite the reference being “partial.” In the edited image, one frog is clearly inside the bowl, but additional frogs are on the lid and floor; the source has no frogs. Do not infer that these extras negate the valid placement—the saved criteria explicitly say they do not—but investigate whether the reference’s partial label reflects another requested criterion or a mismatch in the task/rubric. The current binding (“a frog … inside the toilet”) and s1 criterion encode only that placement, so they cannot distinguish partial from complete under the supplied rubric. Clarify the intended requirement and ensure the executable decision uses all relevant saved support observations before declaring completion; do not invent a frog-count or cleanup requirement from this label alone. The skipped s2 is a conditional dependency, not negative visual evidence, and its transport status should not be treated as a failure. Preserve uncertainty where evidence is insufficient rather than forcing a label.
